docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: This page summarizes the key benchmark results for the FFram project.

docs.title: Metadata Latency (RQ1)
docs.text:
• PyAV: 4.53 ± 0.84 ms per probe.
  • ffprobe: 29.51 ± 2.01 ms per probe.
  • Speedup: 6.51× faster using PyAV.

docs.text: Clip Method CRF Size (KB) VMAF ΔSize High‑motion Static CRF 23 23 5111.7 87.69 – High‑motion Auto‑CRF 15 9257.6 96.58 +81.1 % Low‑motion Static CRF 23 23 37.6 93.16 – Low‑motion Auto‑CRF 17 51.7 96.19 +37.4 % > Interpretation: Auto‑CRF reliably meets the VMAF ≥ 95 target but incurs a size increase; it serves as a quality‑floor rather than a compression optimizer.

docs.title: Research Guide
docs.text: This guide outlines the methodology, experimental design, and reproducibility steps required to produce a rigorous IEEE‑style paper for the FFram project.

docs.title: 1. Research Questions
docs.text:
1. RQ1 – Probing Efficiency: Does native container probing (via PyAV) reduce metadata extraction latency compared to a ffprobe subprocess?
  2. RQ2 – Quality‑Targeted Encoding: Can an automated VMAF‑driven CRF search (Auto‑CRF) reliably achieve a perceptual quality floor while controlling output size?
  3. RQ3 – Parallel Cluster Gains: What speedup does the lightweight XML‑RPC cluster provide relative to single‑node execution?
  4. RQ4 – Fault‑Tolerant Execution: Can rule‑based heuristics recover from out‑of‑memory and GPU‑encoder failures without manual intervention?

docs.title: 2. Experimental Setup
docs.text:
• Hardware: Single workstation (CPU cores, optional GPU). All experiments run on the same machine to isolate algorithmic effects.
  • Software Stack: Python 3.11, FFmpeg with libvmaf, PyAV, standard‑library xmlrpc.
  • Benchmarks:
  • Metadata probe: 20 iterations of a 1‑second synthetic clip.
  • Auto‑CRF: Two synthetic clips (high‑motion, low‑motion) encoded with static CRF 23 and Auto‑CRF targeting VMAF 95.
  • Cluster: Two worker nodes on ports 8001/8002 processing a 4K clip via a segment‑encode‑concatenate pipeline.
  • Resiliency: Fault injection via unittest.mock for OOM and NVENC failures.
  • Metrics: Latency (ms), VMAF score, output size (KB), speedup, efficiency, and success/failure of recovery.

docs.title: 3. Data Collection & Analysis
docs.text:
• Use time.perf_counter for latency measurements.
  • Compute VMAF with libvmaf; report mean ± SD.
  • Size change: (\Delta S = (S_{auto} - S_{static}) / S_{static}).
  • For the cluster, calculate speedup (S(p) = T_1 / T_p) and efficiency (E = S(p) / p).
  • Summarize fault‑injection outcomes (recovery applied vs. not).

docs.title: 4. Reporting Conventions
docs.text:
• Present results in tables and figures with clear captions.
  • Include confidence intervals where appropriate.
  • Discuss internal and external validity threats.
  • Highlight any missing data (e.g., unavailable 4K test video) and its impact on reproducibility.

docs.title: 5. Reproducibility Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] All benchmark scripts are version‑controlled (see website_docs/reference/benchmarks.md).
  • [ ] Exact command lines and library versions are listed in the Environment table.
  • [ ] Random seeds are fixed for deterministic behaviour where applicable.
  • [ ] Raw output logs are archived in the repository's benchmarks/logs/ folder.

Use this guide as a template when extending the paper or adding new experiments.

docs.title: Benchmarks & Performance
docs.text: We regularly benchmark FFram to ensure it maintains high performance, exceptional quality, and robust reliability under pressure.

docs.title: Probe Latency (PyAV vs FFprobe)
docs.text: FFram uses PyAV bindings to instantly extract media metadata instead of spawning slower ffprobe subprocesses for every file. * FFprobe Average Latency: 52.48 ms * PyAV Average Latency: 9.62 ms * Result: FFram metadata probing is 5.46x faster.

docs.title: Auto-Heuristic Resiliency
docs.text: FFram includes self-healing logic for common hardware and system faults. We simulate fatal FFmpeg crashes to ensure pipelines don't fail unexpectedly. * Out-Of-Memory (OOM): When an OOM crash is detected, FFram successfully recovers by applying a -threads 1 fallback parameter. * GPU Encoder Failure (NVENC): If hardware encoding fails (e.g., NVENC driver issues), FFram automatically falls back to CPU encoding (libx264) seamlessly.

docs.title: Auto-CRF & VMAF Quality Control
docs.text: FFram includes smart encoding operations that use VMAF binary search to guarantee perceptual video quality. * High Motion Videos: Reaches a VMAF target of 96.58 by intelligently allocating bandwidth. * Low Motion Videos: Maintains a strict 96.19 VMAF score, preventing quality degradation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.8+
  • FFmpeg installed and available in your system's PATH.

docs.title: Install via Pip
docs.text:
The easiest way to install FFram is via pip:

pip install ffram

docs.title: Install from Source
docs.text:
To install from source for development:

git clone https://github.com/Rebuild-It-Labs/FFram.git
cd FFram
pip install -e .

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
To launch the FFram interactive CLI, simply run:

ffram

If you want to skip the file selection prompt and directly load a video, use the -f flag:

ffram -f "/path/to/my/video.mp4"

docs.title: Basic Operations
docs.text: Once launched, you can navigate the menu using your keyboard arrow keys. Press Enter to select a category, and then select the specific operation you want to run.
